tools.name: post_request
tools.description: The only way to ask this unit for a change. `type` is one of: initiate (start a new project); feature (ask for something the product does not do yet); correction (say that something is wrong); verification (ask for the scenarios that would falsify part of the design); comment (attach a question or observation to part of the design); question (ask something that needs an answer rather than a change). You never name a layer or write an entry -- the type decides how deep the change may reach, and an agent decides what actually changes. `targets` is optional and usually omitted: you are not expected to know how the design is laid out. `title` is the ask in one line and is required; `body` carries the detail; `origin` names who is asking, and is recorded as worded. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: list_requests
tools.description: The request queue. Filter by status, project, type, or target. This is what the processing agent reads to find work.

tools.name: get_request
tools.description: One request, with what it has produced so far.

tools.name: resolve_request
tools.description: Close a request: accepted (with what it produced) or rejected (with why, in `note`). Leaving it pending keeps the queue honest. `produced` is the identifiers this request created, which is what later lets a correction be traced to the request it served. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: create_project
tools.description: Create an empty project. Cite the `initiate` request that authorised it in `in_response_to`. The intent entries themselves arrive as a normal amendment, so they are derived and interviewed for rather than lifted verbatim from whatever the requester typed. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: fork_project
tools.description: Copy a project's live corpus to a new project `name`, so a run works on its own copy and the source stays frozen. Cite an `initiate` request in `in_response_to`. Entries, slices, modules, labels and identifier numbering carry over. Requests, issues, lifecycle events, cuts and emissions do not: a fork starts with none of them, and `left_behind` reports what stayed on the source. `repo` and any delegation are cleared, so a fork cannot ship into the source's tracker until a person points it at one. `name` takes letters, digits, '-' and '_'. An existing name is refused with 409, so a retry after a timeout is safe: check `list_projects`, and a fork that is listed landed. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: submit_amendment
tools.description: Record a batch of derived entries -- the pipeline's own write path. Cite the request it serves in `in_response_to`: an inbox message id, or an issue id (iss-NNNN, open or escalated, this project) when repairing what that issue names. An issue-cited fix starts at the layer of the issue's target and may then propagate downward citing the same issue; one reaching above the target is refused -- escalate the issue instead. Each entry needs a 'layer' and a 'title', and may carry 'body', 'purpose', 'supersedes', and two kinds of edge: 'derives_from' (identifiers exactly one layer up -- what it serves) and 'depends_on' (same layer -- what it needs, and what imposes order). 'emits_into' is refused: the cross-cutting type was removed, and an ambient concern is a foundational slice reached with depends_on. Any other entry field is refused, 'slice' included: the slice is named once, on the amendment. Replacing an entry that sits in a slice needs that amendment-level 'slice', or the replacement would land unassigned. The reply carries `gates_delta` -- sound, complete, and only the findings this amendment `added` or `resolved` -- not the project's whole report; send 'full': true for that as `gates`. A dry run answers the same way. When the amendment cites an issue and is the LAST of its fix, send 'closes_issue': true to close that issue resolved with what it produced (`closed_issue` in the reply). Leave it off until then: a fix propagates downward citing the same issue, and a closed issue can no longer be cited. close_issue remains for already-answered and rejected. Validated as one transaction: an amendment introducing an orphan, a broken horizontal edge, a slice cycle, a spec whose `Imports:` line names an entry it does not depends_on, or a second successor to an id is refused whole, and the first entry created for a request must sit within that request type's permitted origination depth. Entries left unserved are reported, not refused. A supersession strands every entry pointing at what it retired; set 'preserves_interface': true on the replacement when nothing a pointing entry consumed has changed -- a reworded sentence, a stated exemption, an added dependency -- and those edges carry to the replacement instead. That is a judgement about meaning and you are answerable for it: a changed signature, field, return or behaviour is NOT preserving, and claiming it is hides exactly the consumers this graph exists to surface. Either way, every module declared as implementing the retired entry is re-pointed to the replacement in the same write (`repointed_modules`, each {module, was, now}); tests deriving from it and entries depending on it are never rewritten, only listed -- `restate_or_keep` (test ids: restate or keep is your call) and `dependents_stranded` (depends_on the retired entry, not carried because the replacement does not preserve the interface). `same_wave_edges` lists, never refuses, each new entry depending on another slice that sat in the same wave as its own when this was written -- the two were worked side by side, so check what it read was finished. To depend on an entry this same amendment is creating, cite it by position as '#0', '#1' -- a zero-based index into 'entries'. Identifiers are allocated on commit, so guessing one is how a horizontal edge ends up pointing at a real entry that is the wrong entry, which every gate passes. Placeholders work in 'depends_on' only; 'derives_from' points one layer up and an amendment writes one layer, so a sibling is never a parent. 'slice' must name a slice that already exists -- one comes from ratifying a slicing or from split_slice, never from being named here, because slices split and never merge and one created by a typo cannot be undone -- and a test entry takes no slice at all, because its column is the column of the spec entry it derives from. Layer 'T' is a test: one scenario, deriving from exactly one spec entry and carrying no horizontal edge. Its 'purpose' is free text for whoever writes the test; nothing branches on it. `tests_of_dependents` lists the tests of every entry depending, at any distance, on what a supersession retires: their fixtures may assert what you removed, so read them before the cut. **Preview first**: send the same body with `dry_run: true` and you get exactly what this call would answer -- created ids, blast_radius, restate_or_keep, dependents_stranded, tests_of_dependents, repointed_modules, gates, or the refusal with its findings or `reason` -- always status 200 with `admitted` saying what the commit would do, and nothing written, no id allocated, no request or issue touched. A preview also returns `would_ship`: the shipped units whose contract this moves, each {key, number, ship: 'edit' (open issue rewritten) or 'follow_up' (closed completed, so a new issue)}, or null while the change leaves the graph unsound. **Send an `idempotency_key`** (any unique string you choose, e.g. a uuid) on every amendment you might retry: a write can time out and still land, and a blind retry without a key writes the entries twice. A repeat with the same key in this project returns the original answer (same ids, `replayed: true`) and writes nothing; the same key with a different body is a 409. A refused amendment does not use up its key. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: split_slice
tools.description: Move part of a slice out into a NEW slice, named by 'into', carrying the identifiers listed in 'members'. The only correction available to a cut that turned out too coarse: slices split and never merge, because merging destroys identifier locality, so a target that already exists is refused and there is deliberately no operation in the other direction. Nothing is renumbered -- identifiers encode layer and creation order, never slice, so membership moves and every historical reference still resolves. Refused if the split would break the slice structure, which it can: two halves that referred to each other inside one slice become two slices referring to each other, and that may be a cycle. `into` names the new slice and `members` the identifiers moving to it; put the reason in `note`, which is the only record of why a permanent cut was made where it was. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: raise_issue
tools.description: File a request against another slice's entry, then proceed on your own stated assumption. There is no agent-to-agent channel and deliberately so: the agent that wrote the target is gone, and messaging a live one would mean blocking or nondeterminism. `kind` is 'additive' (a new entry is needed; nothing existing changes meaning, so nothing re-runs) or 'semantic' (an existing entry others already consumed now means something else; its consumers are invalidated). That call is a judgement about meaning, so you make it and this unit records it. Put the claim on one line -- the router reads headers only -- and put what you assumed in `assumption`. `raised_by` names the slice or session raising it; `round` is the reconciliation round, omitted unless you are re-raising inside one. **Send an `idempotency_key`** (any unique string, e.g. a uuid) whenever you might retry: a call can time out and still land, and a retry without a key files the issue twice. The same key in this project returns the original issue (same id, `replayed: true`) and files nothing; with a different body it is a 409. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: list_issues
tools.description: The issue queue for a project. Filter by status (open/resolved/escalated/rejected) or by the slice an issue targets.

tools.name: close_issue
tools.description: Move an issue on: resolved (with what it produced), rejected (ruled not a fault, or out of scope -- `note` is the reason and is required), or escalated (it needs a human). An open issue may go to any of the three; an escalated one only to resolved or rejected; resolved and rejected are final. `note` is what the person reading an escalation has to go on. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: get_reconciliation
tools.description: The open issue queue grouped into one repair batch per target slice, in dependency order. Run this after every wave, not once per layer. Each batch carries its re-run scope: the entries that consumed a meaning one of its issues says has moved, computed at entry level, so usually a handful rather than a column. `escalations` are the issues that are not repairs -- past the two-round cap, or semantically reaching back into a wave that is already finished -- and those need a human. This returns the batches as data; running a repair session is the caller's job.

tools.name: get_waves
tools.description: The order the slices may be worked in, computed from the dependency graph rather than chosen. Slices in one wave have no edge between them, so they can be worked in parallel with nothing to coordinate; every earlier wave is complete before the next begins, so each reads its dependencies as frozen. `chain: true` means every wave is one slice wide -- nothing can be done in parallel, and the slices are probably too coupled. `unschedulable` is only non-empty when the gates have already refused the graph.

tools.name: propose_slicing
tools.description: The graph half of the grouping problem, before any slice exists: which behaviours share an intent parent, and how far each parent spreads. A parent whose children scatter widely is either constraint-shaped or evidence the cut runs across the grain of intent -- two opposite readings, which is why it is reported rather than acted on. Grouping by shared nouns is YOUR job: this unit never looks inside a body.

tools.name: score_slicing
tools.description: Score a proposed partition WITHOUT creating it. `proposal` maps slice name to a list of entry ids. Runs every gate and every structural metric as though the cut were real, and commits nothing -- which is what makes trialling several slicings possible, since slices split and never merge. `legal` is computed; good is not. Nothing here gates or refuses anything. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: get_insights
tools.description: Everything measurable about how a project has gone. `change_locality` is the primary score and is not a proxy: a good slicing is one where a typical change lands inside one slice, and every request already records exactly which entries it produced. `corrections` is where defects entered, which reads as a pipeline diagnostic -- clustered at intent means the interview was shallow. Issue pairs measure co-change, but are endogenous: that history was produced under one particular cut. Inputs to a judgement, never a judgement.

tools.name: list_events
tools.description: The project lifecycle in order -- requests as they were actually worded, derivations, corrections and the layer each entered at, refusals, and every assumption an agent had to make because it could not derive something. This is what the graph cannot tell you: a gate that failed and was then fixed leaves no trace in the fixed graph. Pass `since` (a seq) to page. Analysis, not operation -- never load this during ordinary work.

tools.name: get_slice_context
tools.description: One slice assembled for READING: its spec entries with full bodies, the justification chain for each, read-only context from the slices this one depends on (projected from the entries' own edges, never declared beside them). For reviewing or authoring a column, not for building it -- a slice's files are not disjoint from other slices' files, so a slice is not a safe branch scope. Execution scope is a work unit: see get_work_unit. Also carries `scenarios` -- the test entries already written against this column's contracts, spine only, each naming what it judges and whether a file implements it yet -- and `untested`, the contracts with no scenario at all. Read both before writing scenarios: the first is what not to repeat, the second is the work list. Refused if the graph is unsound. Use it as the ONE read before authoring or auditing a slice at a layer, rather than fetching entries one by one: `layer` is B, A, S (default) or T (intent is not sliced); `neighbours` gives each depends_on entry outside the set as its title plus interface lines (Imports, Errors, top-level signatures) and no body; `open_issues` lists the slice's open issues. `max_chars` (default 60000; 0 for no cap) is a budget for the ANCESTORS only: over it, ancestor bodies are dropped from the top layer down, each named in `truncated` (fetch one by id if you need it). `entries` are always whole, so a large slice can exceed the cap; read a big slice's entries with review_layer, which pages.

tools.name: get_work_unit
tools.description: One work unit and everything needed to build it, addressed EITHER by its key, exactly as the unit listing reports it, OR by ANY entry it contains, spec or test. A work unit is ONE spec entry together with every module implementing it -- one unit is one branch and one ticket. A test unit is the scenarios derived from one spec entry and the files implementing those; its key is the spec entry it is anchored to, plus `-T` (`S-01-T`) -- and that key is a key only, never an entry identifier, so pass it as the key. Its `write_set` is module PATHS, and those paths are NOT exclusive: a file implementing several spec entries is written by several units. `overlap` names the units this one shares a file with, and they MUST NOT be worked at the same time. Overlap is not an order -- neither waits for the other and nothing says which goes first -- so it is reported separately from `follows`, and choosing is the caller's job. `file_scope` is the other half of that: for each file in the write set, the other contracts it must eventually serve, with bodies. Read it before designing anything. A unit is one contract but a file is not, and whichever unit reaches a file first decides its shape for all of them. Also carries the entries with full bodies, ONE justification chain for the whole unit -- every entry in a unit shares an anchor and so an ancestry -- a spine-only read set of what it depends on elsewhere, `follows` -- the units this one waits on -- and `size`, for deciding how many units one session should take. A unit holding test modules is one of those: the unit implementing a spec entry follows the unit holding the scenarios derived from it, which is how documentation-first, tests-second, code-last is ordered rather than asked for. `tests` lists the scenarios judging this unit that exist as files, with the paths to run; `tests_pending` lists the ones written but not yet built, which are not yet expected to pass. Computed from the live graph, so it answers what to build now; the stored cut is get_units. Refused if the graph is unsound.

entry.description: A unit key as the listing reports it (`S-01`, `S-01-T`), or any entry the unit contains (`S-01`, `T-30`). Iterating the listing's keys is the normal use and works for both kinds of unit.

tools.name: get_units
tools.description: The current cut -- the work units a person last decided to cut the project into -- plus `drift`, how far the live graph has moved since, and the live projection itself. Drift is one shape rather than a vocabulary: each group names what a set of units `was` and what it is `now`, so a split reads as one was and two now, a merge the reverse, and an empty `now` means gone. That is what answers whether a piece of work is still the same piece. Both the cut and the live projection carry `edges` -- what waits on what, the contract a consumer honours -- and `overlap`, which units share files and so must not run at the same time. Those are different relations: an edge is an order, an overlap is not. `waves` is a view over the edges, with test units shown immediately before the work they precede.

tools.name: list_cuts
tools.description: Every cut taken, oldest first, headers only. Which cut a piece of work came from is answerable only because this exists -- the graph cannot recover it.

tools.name: declare_module
tools.description: Record which spec entries -- or which test entries -- a module implements. The bottom layer's backlink: code is not an entry in this graph, so this is the only thing tying a file to the reasoning that produced it. Replaces rather than merges: declaring an empty list removes the module. Spec and test identifiers are accepted, but never together in one module: a a unit's write set is every module implementing ITS OWN entries, so a file claiming both kinds would put the test file inside the implementation unit's write set -- letting the agent edit the tests that judge it. A module claiming an architecture entry is refused outright -- it has skipped the layer that says how. `path` is the file, repository-relative, and is what a work unit hands out as its write set. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: list_modules
tools.description: Every module backlink, and every relation computable from it. Each row carries `slices` -- which slices the file reaches, most-represented first, because a file may serve more than one and a single value would be an assertion rather than a fact -- and one link direction: `covers` on a test file (the implementation files holding the contracts its tests judge) or `covered_by` on an implementation file (the test files judging its contracts). Both are computed from the graph and stored nowhere, so they cannot fall out of step with `implements`. Three reports: `untested`, contracts nothing says how to falsify; `unimplemented_tests`, tests written but not yet built, which order nothing and are not yet expected to pass; and `uncovered_tests`, test files judging a contract nobody has built. For spec entries no module implements, read `unimplemented` from get_units -- an entry nothing implements is exactly an entry in no work unit.

tools.name: get_plan
tools.description: The spec-level diff since a mark, resolved into a write set (modules implementing a changed entry -- editable) and a read set (modules that consumed a changed meaning but did not themselves change -- context only). `since` is the `mark` a previous plan returned; omit it for a first iteration, where the whole spec layer is the diff. This is the planner's input, and deliberately NOT a git diff: reasoning from code makes code the source of truth and the spec layer decorative within a few cycles. Refused while the graph is unsound.

tools.name: audit_diff
tools.description: Compare the files actually touched against the write set that was declared. This is where a git diff belongs -- afterwards, as evidence rather than as input. YOU run git and pass the paths in `touched`; this unit never executes anything. Pass `editable_paths`, or pass `since` and let it derive them. A file touched outside the set is a gate failure: either the planner missed a dependency or the executor freelanced. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: record_audit
tools.description: Record that you ran an audit, once per run, as soon as it ends. Record a PASS too: an audit that found nothing leaves no other trace, and an unrecorded pass is indistinguishable from an audit that never ran. `scope` is what you audited -- entry ids and/or `slice:<name>`. `layer` is the layer letter you audited, or `slice`, `final` or `delta`. `questions` are the ids of the audit questions you asked (e.g. S1, T4). `outcome` is `pass` or `flagged`; when flagged, raise each problem with raise_issue FIRST and list the iss-NNNN ids in `issues` (empty on a pass). The one exception is a `slice` audit, whose findings go to a person rather than onto entries: it may flag with no issues if `note` says what was flagged. `note` is optional free text otherwise. `auditor` and `run_id` are free text naming you and the run. This stores references only: it never judges, scores or gates anything, and refuses only a name that does not exist. Read audits back with list_events, kind `audit`. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: review_layer
tools.description: Read one layer with each entry's justification chain, what serves it, and the comments attached to it -- so a reviewer sees the decision and what it claims to serve in one place. `layer` is one of I (intent), B (behaviour), A (architecture), S (spec), T (test). T reads the scenarios, which is where the second source of truth gets reviewed. `gates` is the check_gates report narrowed to the entries on this page; at S, `unknown_member` and `undefined_name` are where sibling contracts disagree on a shared interface. Paged: a reply stays under `max_chars` (default 60000; 0 for no cap) and gives `next_after` -- pass it back as `after` for the next page; null means the last page. Pass `slice` to read one column at a time.

tools.name: get_spine
tools.description: Every entry's identifier, one-line title and all three edge lists, with no bodies. Load this first, decide from the structure what you need, then fetch those bodies by identifier. `layer` is one of I (intent), B (behaviour), A (architecture), S (spec), T (test); omit it for the whole graph. Filtering to T is how you see which scenarios already exist before writing more.

tools.name: get_entry
tools.description: One entry's full body, its parents, and what derives from it.

tools.name: check_gates
tools.description: Soundness and completeness. Sound means nothing is malformed and nothing is half-corrected; unsound blocks work. Complete means no findings at all -- knowledge has reached spec on every branch and every contract can be caught failing; incomplete is the to-do list and blocks nothing. Blocking kinds: `orphan` (derives from something missing, sideways, or nothing at all), `bad_dependency`, `stranded`, `bad_import` (a spec's `Imports:` line names an entry it has no depends_on edge to), and two read against the module map: `bad_module_import` (an imported module nobody declares, or whose implementer is not depended on) and `undeclared_path` (a spec names a file under a code root that no module declares). `split_ownership` (a file implemented from two slices) is reported, never blocking, and so is `two_successors` (two entries supersede one id): the amendment that would add the second claim is refused, but a fork already in the append-only history cannot be repaired and leaves the graph sound. The module-map kinds refuse cuts and plans, not amendments: a module is declared after the entry it implements exists. `stranded` is the one to read differently: it means a parent was RETIRED and the finding names the successor, so nothing is malformed -- a correction landed and has not been carried down yet. It blocks because work must not be issued from a spec citing a retired contract, but the remedy is to re-derive, not to repair. Correcting a TESTED spec entry strands its scenarios; re-pointing them is a follow-on `verification` request, because an amendment writes one layer. Reporting kinds, which never block: `unserved`, `untested`, `no_imports_line` (a spec without the line, once the project writes it elsewhere), `split_ownership`, and five read out of code (approximations -- each detail says what to check): `undefined_name` (a spec imports or types over a name no live spec defines in a code block), `unknown_member` (a spec reads `x.attr` where the class another spec declares has no such member), `sweep_collision` (a spec's test sweeps a directory for tokens a sibling's code there must use; both are named), and `no_module` (a spec no module implements, once the project declares modules -- it is in no work unit, so no ticket carries it). Plus `undeclared_test_path` (a test body names a file under a declared module's top directory that no module declares, so the test unit cannot create it; a directory counts as declared when a declared module lives under it) -- reported here, and only refused by auto_ship's `tests_assigned`. `cosmetic` lists `retired_mention` (a live body citing a retired id; tickets render it `S-02 (was S-01)`) and `unlinked_mention` (a body naming an id it has no edge to). Neither counts against `complete`, and neither needs a re-issue.

tools.name: submit_proposal
tools.description: Submit a proposed slicing for ratification: a mapping of slice name to the entry identifiers it would own, and a note carrying the rationale. Creates nothing -- a partition is not a partition until a human rules on it. While a proposal is pending no further slicing session is dispatched. An entry proposed for two slices is refused here rather than at the ratification gate. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: get_proposal
tools.description: The slicing proposal currently awaiting ratification, if any, with the note that came with it and the reason the last one was rejected. `status` is 'pending' or 'none'.

tools.name: list_projects
tools.description: Every project this unit holds.

tools.name: get_emission
tools.description: How far an emission of this project's work units into its issue tracker has got, and what previous runs created. `running` says whether one is in flight; when it is, `processed` of `total` is the progress and `phase` is `creating` or `wiring`. That run status is in memory and a restart erases it. The durable answer for a run id is its lifecycle event: done = a `tickets_emitted` event with that `run_id`, failed = a `ship_failed` event with that `run_id` (`error` or `reason`), both read with list_events (`GET /projects/{project}/events?kind=...`) and both surviving a restart. `emissions` lists completed runs from the durable emission log. `already` maps the units of the CURRENT cut that have issues to those issues -- so the number a run would newly create is the cut's units minus these, which is not the same as the unit count and is the number worth knowing before starting one. `token` says whether this unit holds a tracker token at all -- a boolean, never the value, and the one precondition nothing in the project can answer. `build` is the commit this process serves (null if unknown). `shipped` is what a `shipped` press would create (`create`, keys) and how many units it would hold (`held`), null while a run is in flight. `unassigned_tests` (T ids no test module declares, so no test unit carries them) and `undeclared_test_paths` (`[{t, path}]`, files a T names that no module declares, so no write set can create them) are what this press would ship without tests; always present, empty when clean, never a refusal. Starting an emission is a person's decision and is not offered here -- except under a delegation, through auto_ship.

tools.name: check_ship_access
tools.description: Ask GitHub, now, whether this unit's token is live and can write to the project's repository -- before a Ship or an auto_ship. `ok` true means both; otherwise `reason` says which failed: no token, no repo, a token GitHub rejects (expired, revoked, mistyped), a repo the token cannot see, or read-only access (issues carry labels, which need write access). Also `identity` (the account issues will be authored by) and `push`. Read-only: it changes nothing and refuses nothing. The token is never returned.

tools.name: get_delegation
tools.description: Whether a person has delegated Ship for this project to agents: `delegation.enabled`, with who granted or revoked it (`actor`), when (`at`) and their `note`. Never granted reads as `enabled: false`. Granting is a person's decision and is not offered here; check this before calling auto_ship.

tools.name: auto_ship
tools.description: Cut the project and Ship it, on your own judgement, under a person's standing delegation (D2). Use it after a repair you made at S or T to units already on the tracker. It does nothing and answers 409 unless ALL hold, reported per name in `conditions` and listed in `failed`: `delegation` (granted and not revoked), `ready` (repo set, token held, no press in flight), `gates` (graph sound, modules declared, no dead-end citation, no loop in the units' own edges, no shipped unit waiting on a blocker with no live issue), `st_only` (since the cut the last press shipped, no I, B or A entry was added or superseded), `shipped` (every unit the change touches -- entries or edges -- already has an issue) and `tests_assigned` (no live T is in no test module -- `unassigned_tests` -- and no T names a file no module declares -- `undeclared_test_paths`, `[{t, path}]`; declare_module them first). A refusal is final for you: it is the person's press, so stop and say which condition failed, never work around it. When all hold it takes a cut and presses Ship exactly as the person's buttons do, except that it never creates an issue for a unit with none: it edits, follows up and withdraws. Answers 202 with a `run_id` (progress via get_emission) and `cut_seq`. Every finished run writes exactly one lifecycle event carrying that `run_id`: done = a `tickets_emitted` event, failed (it raised, `error`, or refused, `reason`) = a `ship_failed` event. Read them with list_events (`GET /projects/{project}/events?kind=tickets_emitted` or `?kind=ship_failed`); both survive a restart, while the in-flight run status in get_emission does not. `note` is kept on the cut and the `auto_ship` event. Send `actor` (your session or agent name): every write is logged under it.

tools.name: get_labels
tools.description: The labels added to every issue this project's work units become -- on top of the per-unit ones naming the anchor, the kind and each slice. Project-wide operating config, typically naming the team a consumer admits work for, and the reason a consumer can have one admission rule covering both generated issues and ones a person filed by hand. Also `pickup`: the labels a consumer adds when it picks an issue up. An issue carrying one is never edited or closed by a Ship, and with none configured nothing is edited.

tools.name: get_repo
tools.description: The repository this project's work units become tickets in, as `owner/name`. `null` means none is configured, which is a normal answer and not a fault -- but nothing can be emitted until one is.
